q: To whom is a designer responsible according to C1.1.1?
a: Clients, their community and the environment. The designer must balance these when they compete, as a continuing commitment (Kaizen), not a one-off.

q: What resources must a designer use rationally?
a: Materials, manufacturing processes, energy, and recyclability and reusability.

q: What is Kaizen and who introduced it in Japan?
a: Japanese for continuous improvement: small gradual changes tested on a small scale. W. Edwards Deming introduced it in 1950s post-war Japan, building on Shewhart's PDSA cycle.

q: What do the letters PDCA stand for?
a: Plan, Do, Check, Act. It developed from Shewhart's PDSA: Plan, Do, Study, Act.
Our Common Future (1987), by the UN World Commission on Environment and Development chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland. It popularised sustainable development.

q: What do circular economy principles lead to?
a: More durable, repairable and recyclable products, with a positive impact on people, planet and profit.

q: Why are PFAS, PCBs and dioxin called forever chemicals?
a: They resist degradation and accumulate in groundwater, causing health problems. PFAS from firefighting foam has contaminated groundwater.

q: What figures does Metcalfe give for fast fashion?
a: Criticised as contributing up to 8-10 percent of global CO2, with about 87 percent of textile waste going to landfill each year.

q: What is a product standard? Give a toy example.
a: A documented guideline specifying technical requirements for safety, quality, consistency and suitability. Examples: ASTM F963 (USA) and ISO 8124-1 for toy safety.

Standardisation is establishing common practices, methods or formats (e.g. weights and measures). Interchangeability is the result: parts from different makers can replace each other (e.g. bolts of a marked property class).

q: Who pioneered interchangeable parts and when?
a: Gribeauval (France, 1776, artillery), Honore Blanc (1778, flintlock musket using jigs and gauges), then Hall, North and Blanchard (USA, 1816-1818, mechanised mass production).

q: Define planned obsolescence and give three of its design features.
a: A deliberate tactic to give products a limited lifespan, forcing repeat purchase. Features: low durability, style obsolescence, hard or costly to repair, hard to disassemble, regular new improved models.

q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of planned obsolescence.
a: Advantage: consumers can upgrade to new technology, and volume sales support the economy and jobs. Disadvantage: constant replacement, poor repairability and more waste, pollution and resource use.

q: Distinguish style, functional and technological obsolescence.
a: Style: works but no longer fashionable (bell-bottoms). Functional: outdated design or features reduce usefulness (house layout, old phone). Technological: replaced by better technology (CRT to LCD).
Named after Thorstein Veblen (1857-1929): a higher price raises demand because price signals quality and conspicuous consumption brings social prestige.

q: What is a fad? Give two examples from Metcalfe.
a: A very short-lived fashion trend adopted quickly and dropped quickly. Examples: Pet Rocks (1975), Beanie Babies, Tamagotchi, troll dolls.

q: What happened in the DGCCRF Apple case (7 February 2020)?
a: iOS updates could slow iPhone 6, SE and 7 models with old batteries. After a 2017 complaint by HOP, Apple accepted a settlement: EUR 25 million plus a statement on its website for one month, for misleading commercial practice.

q: What does the EU common charger rule require, and from when?
a: USB-C as the common port for phones, tablets, headphones and similar devices since 28 December 2024, and for laptops since 28 April 2026. Devices can be sold without chargers. Estimated about 980 tonnes less e-waste and at least EUR 250 million saved per year.
